title: IELTS Speaking — Practice Test 28
topics: A story an older relative told you
Memory, elders and what gets passed down

questions: Does your name have a meaning, or a story behind why you were given it?
Do people usually call you by your full name, or a shorter version or nickname?
Why do you think parents in your country choose the names they do?
Are the names popular now different from the names common in your grandparents' time?
If you had children one day, would you pick a traditional name or something modern?
Are there any stories that get told again and again in your family — at dinners, at festivals?
Who is the storyteller in your family, the one everyone listens to?
Why do you think families enjoy retelling the same stories they've all heard before?
Did you hear more family stories as a child than you do now?
Do you think the stories from your family will still be told a generation from now?

part2.title: Describe a story an older person in your family told you.
bullets: who told you the story and when they told it
why they told it to you
how you reacted when you heard it
part2.explain: and explain why this story has stayed with you, and whether you have passed it on to anyone else.
followups: Do you think the story is completely true, or has it grown in the telling?
Is that person still able to tell you stories now?
Are there other stories from them you wish you had asked about?

part3.q: What can a grandparent's story give us that a history book about the same period cannot?
followups: Is there anything the history book does better?
Which would you trust more on the details?

part3.q: Why do you think so many people only become curious about their family's past after the older generation has gone?
followups: Have you noticed this in your own family?
What could prompt people to ask earlier?

part3.q: What kinds of things get lost when stories pass from one generation to the next?
followups: Is anything gained in the retelling?
Does it matter if the facts drift, as long as the meaning survives?

part3.q: Families in many countries are becoming smaller and more spread out. How does that change the way family memory works?
followups: Can phone calls and visits do what living together used to do?
Is this change worse for some cultures than others?

part3.q: In some cultures elders are treated as authorities; in others, old age brings much less status. What explains the difference?
followups: Which way is your own country moving?
Does economic change play a part?

part3.q: When societies modernise quickly, the knowledge of older people can start to look out of date. Is respect for elders still justified when their advice no longer applies?
followups: Is there a kind of knowledge that doesn't go out of date?
How can generations stay useful to each other despite this?

part3.q: We now have endless photos and videos of family life on our phones. Does all that recording actually help us remember?
followups: What's the difference between a recording of a moment and a memory of it?
Will today's children be glad of those archives or overwhelmed by them?

part3.q: Some people record interviews with their grandparents; others say a story loses something the moment a camera appears. Which side are you on?
followups: What exactly changes when someone knows they're being recorded?
Is an imperfect recording still better than nothing?

part3.q: Oral traditions carried entire cultures for thousands of years before writing. Do you think something of that skill has been lost for good?
followups: Where, if anywhere, does oral storytelling still thrive today?
Could it matter in a digital age, or is this just nostalgia?

part3.q: A century from now, will people know more about our generation's ordinary lives than we know about our great-grandparents' — or less, because so much digital data will be unreadable or deleted?
followups: Who should be responsible for preserving ordinary people's records?
Would you want your own descendants to see everything you've posted?

fc: Retells someone else's story in Part 2 without losing the thread — story-within-a-story structure is the specific fluency challenge of this card.
Signals the layers clearly ("the way my grandmother told it…", "apparently…", "and this is the part I still find hard to believe") so the listener always knows whose voice we're in.
Moves between the past of the story, the moment of telling, and the present reflection without tense-driven stumbles breaking the flow.
In Part 3, builds comparisons (oral vs. written, recorded vs. remembered) in organised steps rather than bouncing between sides.
Uses natural fillers of thought ("how do I put this…") instead of silence when the abstract memory questions bite.
lr: Storytelling and memory vocabulary: hand down, pass on, fade, vivid, exaggerate, embellish, word of mouth, keep a story alive.
Family and generation range: ancestors, descendants, upbringing, extended family, family lore, the older generation, skip a generation.
Reported speech vocabulary varies naturally: she swore that, he used to claim, apparently, the way she told it, or so the story goes.
Part 3 abstraction is available when needed: oral tradition, collective memory, archive, heritage, continuity, digital footprint.
Distinguishes shades precisely: remember vs. reminisce, story vs. account, respect vs. reverence, old vs. elderly vs. elder.
gra: Past perfect anchors the story-behind-the-story: "she was describing something that had happened forty years before I was born".
Reported speech is controlled across tenses: "he told me they had walked for three days", "she always said she would never go back".
used to and would paint the era the story comes from: "in her village they would fetch water before dawn".
Comparative structures carry Part 3: "far more intimate than a textbook", "the less families live together, the fewer stories survive".
Hedged speculation for the future questions: "much of today's data may well be unreadable", "I suspect our grandchildren will know oddly little about us".
pron: Shifts voice subtly when quoting the older relative — a slight change of pace or pitch for reported lines lifts the whole Part 2.
Emotive stress lands where the story turns: "they lost EVERYTHING that night — and she never once complained about it."
Multi-syllable topic words are secure: generation, ancestors, tradition, nostalgia, inheritance — stress in the right place.
Pace slows at the story's weightiest moment instead of rushing past it; silence used deliberately is a pronunciation feature, not a fault.
Weak forms keep narration natural: "she_used_to tell_us", "one_of_the stories" — full-strength function words make storytelling sound robotic.

band9.part1: Answer the question, then attach one true detail. For "Does your name have a meaning, or a story behind why you were given it?" a Band 9 answer sounds like: "It does — I'm named after my grandfather, who died the year before I was born. My mother says it wasn't even discussed; everyone simply assumed." Two sentences, a real family fact, natural reported speech — not an etymology lecture.
part2: Frame the telling first — who told you, roughly when, and the scene: a power cut, a long train ride, the kitchen after a festival meal. The setting of the telling is half this card.
Tell the story itself in miniature — beginning, turn, ending in four or five sentences. It's their story, so 'apparently' and 'the way he told it' keep the layers clear.
Include one line in their voice — a sentence of reported or direct speech ("she'd say: we were poor, but so was everyone, so nobody noticed") makes the person audible.
Explain why they told it — the third bullet: a warning, a lesson, pride, or just the mood of the evening. Guessing honestly ("I think she needed someone to know") works beautifully.
Give your reaction then and your understanding now — as a child you laughed; now you hear what it cost them. That double perspective is Band 9 material on this card.
Close on the explain line — why it stayed with you, and whether you've passed it on; if you haven't, say who you're saving it for.

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: We now have endless photos and videos of family life on our phones. Does all that recording actually help us remember?
framework: Answer: commit to a side — e.g. mostly no; we've confused capturing moments with keeping them.
Explain: give the mechanism — knowing the camera has it, the mind files the moment as saved and stops doing the work of remembering; ten thousand unsorted photos are a landfill, not an archive.
Example: one concrete illustration — most people can retell their grandmother's story heard once by firelight, but can't say what's in last year's camera roll without scrolling.
Alternative view: concede genuinely — a recording holds what memory cannot: her actual voice, his exact laugh; for families separated by distance or bereavement, that is beyond price.

Evaluate: land the judgement — recording helps when it's deliberate and rare, a few treasures someone curates; it fails as a substitute for the retelling, because memory lives in repetition, not storage.

mistakes.title: Describing the grandparent instead of the story
mistakes.detail: The card asks for a story they told, not a portrait of the person. Candidates spend ninety seconds on how kind their grandmother was and never actually recount anything. The examiner needs a tale with a beginning and an end.

mistakes.title: Choosing a story with no shape
mistakes.detail: "He told me about his village life" is a topic, not a story. Pick one incident — the flood, the wedding that nearly didn't happen, the journey with one suitcase — something that can be ruined by interruption. That's the test of whether it's a story.

mistakes.title: Losing control of the time layers
mistakes.detail: This card has three time zones: when the events happened, when you were told, and now. Jumping between them without past perfect or clear markers ("years later, when she finally told me…") turns the answer into a tense salad.

mistakes.title: Ignoring 'why they told it to you'
mistakes.detail: The third bullet is the card's soul — stories are told for reasons: to warn, to teach, to be remembered. Candidates who skip it deliver a plot summary and miss the easiest source of depth on the whole card.

mistakes.title: Forgetting reported speech entirely
mistakes.detail: A story heard from someone else begs for 'she said', 'he swore', 'apparently'. Telling it entirely in flat third-person past wastes the exact grammar range this card was designed to elicit.

mistakes.title: Only talking about your own family in Part 3
mistakes.detail: Part 3 moves from your grandmother to grandmothers in general. Questions about elders across cultures and shrinking families need 'in many societies', 'urban families tend to' — your family appears as one example, briefly.

mistakes.title: Sentimentality instead of analysis
mistakes.detail: "Old people are treasures and we must respect them" answers nothing. The question is why status differs across cultures and what happens as societies modernise — it wants causes and consequences, not greeting-card lines.

mistakes.title: Claiming technology preserves everything
mistakes.detail: The final questions are sharper than 'phones are good for memories'. Band 8–9 candidates notice the catch: formats die, accounts get deleted, and nobody curates ten thousand photos. Engage with the doubt built into the question.

mistakes.title: Overusing 'in the past' as a time frame
mistakes.detail: Six answers all opening with "In the past, people…" flattens your range. Vary the anchors: a couple of generations ago, before smartphones, in my grandparents' day, when extended families still lived under one roof.

mistakes.title: Rushing the emotional centre of the story
mistakes.detail: Candidates sprint past the very moment that makes the story worth telling — the loss, the reunion, the punchline — as if embarrassed by it. Slowing down there is where Fluency, Pronunciation and the story itself all score together.
